entry.title: Paper accepted at STI-ENID 2026
entry.content:
The paper “Dimensions of Diversity and Their Effects on Citation Impact: Evidence from Philosophy of Science”, which I co-authored with my master student Guglielmo Sproloquio, has been accepted for presentation at the 30th Annual International Conference on Science and Technology Indicators! The paper is our first application of SOPHIS data to address a research question: do publications authored by diverse teams in philosophy of science attract more citations than publications authored by homogeneous teams?

The conference, themed Indicators for a Responsible Research Future, will take place at the University of Antwerp (Belgium) from 9 to 11 September 2026 and wil bring together leading experts, researchers, and policymakers to explore how science, technology, and innovation (STI) indicators can advance responsible research and innovation (RRI). Key topics will include diversity, inclusivity, openness, and sustainability in research assessment and policy.

Here’s the abstract of the paper:

Diversity is becoming a central concern for science policy, both as a matter of equity and as a potential driver of innovation. However, existing scientometric studies on diversity have mainly focused on natural and social sciences, leaving the humanities underexplored. This paper addresses this gap by focusing on philosophy of science, a field in which the epistemic benefits of diversity have been extensively theorized. Using data from the SOPHIS database and OpenAlex, we examine three dimensions of intra-team diversity—gender, institutional, and disciplinary—and their association with citation impact in philosophy of science. Results show that only disciplinary diversity is positively and significantly associated with citation impact. Interaction analyses further reveal that diversity dimensions do not operate independently. While diversity is often promoted as a general driver of scientific excellence, our findings suggest that the impact of diversity is dimension-specific and context-dependent.

entry.title: Visiting professorship in Bochum
entry.content:
Between April and July 2026, I will be DAAD Guest Professor at the Ruhr University Bochum in Germany! I will be hosted by the Institute for Philosophy II under the Chair of Social Epistemology and Philosophy of Science led by Prof. Dunja Šešelja.

I will teach 3 courses for students of Philosophy and Cognitive Sciences:

  • Data Science for Philosophy (30h, standard lectures)
  • Scientometrics and Science Mapping (30h, standard lectures)
  • Quantitative Studies of Philosophy (30h, block seminar)

Visit the Teaching page for courses’ materials and updates.

entry.title: SOPHIS paper out in Scientometrics
entry.content:
A new paper is out! “SOPHIS: an open-access database for quantitative studies of contemporary philosophy of science”, has been published today in Scientometrics in open access!

The SOPHIS database described in the paper (acronym for Social Observatory of PHIlosophy of Science) is the result of two years of hard work. It involved extensive manual data collection (we had to open and browse the PDFs of more than 6,000 articles), followed by painstaking and intensive data cleaning. Both the paper and the database are now freely available in open access to the research community. We hope they will become a standard infrastructure for quantitative research in philosophy of science.

Last but not least, I’m especially proud of this paper because it is the first one I have co-authored with my wife, Selene, who brilliantly designed the graph version of SOPHIS!

entry.title: UniTO Working Group on Open Science

link.title: UniTO Working Group on Open Science

entry.content:
I have been officially appointed as an expert member of the Working Group on Open Science at the University of Turin. I have been appointed as an expert in “quantitative analysis of science, science policy and mapping of scientific systems”.

The Working Group supports the development of open science practices at the university, contributing to the drafting of institutional policies and to the implementation of the National Open Science Plan (part of the National Research Program 2021-2027). The Working Group includes researchers from a wide array of disciplines, from life sciences to archaeology, from computer science to physics.

I am particularly interested in open science and research evaluation and open data management.

entry.title: Workshop Philosophy of Science meets Quantitative Studies of Science

link.title: Workshop Philosophy of Science meets Quantitative Studies of Science

entry.content:
On May 27, 28, and 29 2024 I organized the international workshop Philosophy of Science meets Quantitative Studies of Science at the University of Turin, featuring key figures from both scientometrics and philosophy of science.

Participants to the workshop

Description of the workshop

Philosophy of science and quantitative studies of science (scientometrics and bibliometrics) are currently distinct fields with limited interactions. However, they share numerous objects of investigation and areas of potential common interest. Recent works on disruption indicators for individuating scientific breakthroughs , for instance, address classic philosophy of science topics, such as scientific revolutions and scientific progress, from a quantitative perspective. But also research evaluation, an area in which scientometric indicators play a central role in many countries, would benefit from a closer collaboration between philosophers of science and quantitative researchers, especially to better understand how and to what extent metrics can accelerate or hinder the production of good science .

While quantitative studies of science and philosophy of science are currently distant, this wasn’t always the case. In the early days of scientometrics, quantitative researchers looked to philosophy of science for theories of scientific change and science structure (Small, 2003) and leading philosophers of science, such as Thomas Kuhn, were interested in the pioneering quantitative analyses of scientific networks. The Workshop Philosophy of Science Meets Quantitative Studies of Science aims to reignite the dialogue between philosophers of science and quantitative researchers by inviting leading experts in the two fields to discuss shared topics of interest.
